html:
The fourth ecumenical council of the Christian church, held at Chalcedon, across the Bosporus from Constantinople, from October to November 451. It was called by the emperor Marcian and his wife Pulcheria, and more than 500 bishops attended, the largest council of the age.

It dealt with the question of how Christ is both God and man. It rejected Eutyches, who saw only one nature in Christ after the union, and confirmed the condemnation of Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus. Leaning on a letter from Pope Leo I, it defined Christ as one person in two natures, divine and human, "without confusion, without change, without division, without separation".

Many Christians in Egypt, Syria and Armenia refused this formula, which they thought went back toward Nestorius. Their churches became the Oriental Orthodox family, a split that lasts today. Emperors tried for two centuries to heal it, for example with the Henotikon of 482, and failed.
